Question: I just had a rand new roof put on my home but I still smell a moldy smell whenever it rains. What could it be?

Question: What causes water pipes to burst in winter?
Answer: When water freezes, it expands. Since water is essentially incompressible, when a short section has an ice block growing in one end and the other end blocked by a valve or faucet, the pressure in that section skyrockets. We instrumented this in the 1970s and in a 1-inch steel pipe (typical of a feed to a house) we were able to achieve well over 1000 psi. When residential piping is rated at 150 maximum psi, it is pretty obvious that a burst is simple to achieve.

Question: How does Himalayan pink salt differ from regular table salt?
Answer: Salt, “sodium chloride,” is naturally snow white. So if the salt is pure, it is white. Himalayan pink salt is pink because it contains pink dirt. Most of the dirt, by analysis, is rust. Fact. “But it’s loaded with valuable minerals” Horse crap. Analysis shows that there isn’t enough of any mineral to be of health significance to a human. You’d have to consume a fatal dose of this dirty salt to get any benefits from it. “But since the crystals are larger, less salt fits in a teaspoon, so you’re eating less sodium.” <slaps forehead> Correct, genius, if less salt fits in your teaspoon because the rest of the space is air, you’re consuming less salt/sodium. Buy your table salt with a coarser grind. No dirt. “But I like the flavor difference.” Most of us grow out of eating dirt, boogers, and library paste. Whatever makes your boat float, I guess. “I like it because it’s less processed.” Processed is a dirty word, literally. The processing of salt is for one purpose — getting rid of the dirt. Nothing is added. Nothing but dirt is taken away. “It’s better because it doesn’t have any additives.” Wait. Wut? What about all of that added dirt? It’s true that no modern company added the dirt but it’s still something foreign added to the sodium chloride. The only additives in plain pure table salt are a safe agent to keep the naturally hygroscopic sodium chloride from turning itself into a solid lump inside your salt shaker, or, in some countries, an iodine compound is added to keep you from developing a nasty ugly affliction called “goiter.” In a few countries, they’ve started to add a fluoride compound to keep the teeth from falling out of your crotch fruit or end up with a mouth full of cavities like you or your parents had. Finally, in most countries, the Himalayan stuff is grotesquely more expensive. That’s a difference. If you’re in one of the rare locations where the pink stuff is the same price as the pure stuff, I’d seriously look at the price of the pure stuff. Somebody is ripping you off.

Question: How long does it take plastic to off gas? I was told the fumes of new plastic is harmful. How long until they go away?
Answer: First, some plastics don’t off-gas at all. Some don’t off-gas outside of the first few minutes in the factory. Some only off-gas if they’re processed incorrectly. The most notorious plastics are spray foam insulations. Even the new ones require 1–3 days of excellent ventilation. The old urea formaldehyde spray foams could emit for a long time, were notably toxic, and are now banned. Polyester or vinyl ester “fiberglassing” systems vary widely with off-gas properties ranging from a couple of hours for a single layer that is completely reacted to many days for thick sections that are not heat treated. There are so many variables from plastic type to type, how it’s used, how it’s post-cure processed, and the environment that only the manufacturer can possibly predict this. Ask them.

Question: How are metal shims made?
Answer: I’m not sure how they’re commercially manufactured but on an artisan level, they’re made using a rolling mill where a bar of metal is run between two powerful rollers that squeeze the metal thinner. Once thinned a bit the rollers are forced slightly closer together and the thinned bar is run through the rollers again, squeezing it to thinner still. This is repeated until the desired shim thickness is achieved. This is a small shop’s soft metal “roll”. (The lower set of rolls is for rolling shapes to create wires and small rods.) Hard metal shims like steel require even more massive rolls and motor power.

Question: Can tequila be stored in a plastic water bottle? If so, how long?
Answer: That depends on the water bottle. Back in the days when there weren’t crazy people running around, we could carry just about anything onto an airplane. My work partner and I had flown into Puerto Rico to work our industrial “magic” at a chemical plant out in the rural southern coast. We did well and developed a camaraderie with a group of the plant workers. On our final day, their foreman showed up with a jug of the local white lightning as a going away gift to us. Mighty powerful stuff. One sip and your mouth, throat, and gut were asking, “Why did you do that to me?” They gave us the whole gallon and we headed out for San Juan to catch our plane back home. How were we going to lug a glass gallon jug onto the plane? As we got close to San Juan there were a bunch of tourist trinket shops and one had some faux pirate canteens in leather pouches with shoulder straps showing in the window. We stopped and bought one. In the parking lot, we filled the canteen to its probably 16-ounce brim then bid farewell to the jug and its remaining “joy juice”. At the airport, we split up — I was headed to Chicago and my partner was headed to New York. He took the canteen of hooch, thankfully probably relieving me of a future epic hangover. When I got back to the office the next day, there was a telex waiting for me (I told you this was a long time ago.) My partner had nearly been arrested. He had stowed the canteen in the plane’s overhead compartment for his trip. Unbeknownst to us, the “canteen” was formed of two halves of a plastic bottle shape, glued together. Somewhere, out over the Atlantic, the “juice” had eaten the glue, the bottle exploded apart, and a shower of powerful alcohol ensued. The other passengers and stewardesses were NOT amused. So, if you’re going to put tequila into a plastic container, check the seams, the grade of plastic, and its resistance to alcohol.
